extracted.intended_audience: general public; student journalists; school administrators; legal advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal and practical standards governing when schools may control or shut down student newspapers, with relevant case law, constitutional protections, and common administrative practices cited. Useful for understanding when censorship may be unlawful and what defenses or limits exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tinker standard for student speech
rubrics_metrics.description: "Students do not lose their First Amendment freedoms on school grounds" (Tinker v. Des Moines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Tinker, student speech is protected so long as it is lawful, peaceful, and does not result in a "serious disruption of normal school activity." The page cites SPLC commentary that — before Hazelwood — the bar was that speech must not cause a serious disruption to be censored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazelwood deference to school editorial control
rubrics_metrics.description: School boards have "wide authority to censor school newspapers" when the publication is school-sponsored and censorship is reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns (Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educators may exercise editorial control over style and content of student speech in school-sponsored expressive activities so long as actions are reasonably related to legitimate pedagogical concerns. Applies especially to student media that are part of curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint discrimination prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Government (school) actions that suppress expression merely because public officials oppose a speaker's view constitute viewpoint discrimination and may violate the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACLU and SPLC argued the Viking Saga shutdown was viewpoint discrimination. Judge Gerrard's opinion warned that policies or decisions to restrict speech that 'reflect an effort to suppress expression merely because the public officials oppose a speaker's view' may run afoul of the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing / injury requirement for plaintiffs
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff must demonstrate an injury or ongoing harm to have standing to challenge a school's actions in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lawsuit on behalf of Marcus Pennell was dismissed because the judge found Pennell had already graduated and thus could not prove injury (lacked standing). The dismissal was narrowly focused on standing rather than the substantive constitutional question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX as a potential protection against discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions that target or discriminate against students on the basis of sex/gender (including sexual orientation/gender identity) may implicate Title IX protections against sexual discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ACLU argued shutting down the paper violated students' First and Fourteenth Amendment rights, as well as Title IX protections. Title IX may be invoked where censorship is part of discriminatory treatment of LGBTQ students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private/independent schools may have fewer constitutional protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers at independent (private) schools may enjoy fewer constitutional protections than papers at public schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators noted that some independent high school papers (e.g., The Forum, Midway) are unusual in not being subject to administrative censorship; private-school status can reduce First Amendment constraints on administrators compared to public-school settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliminating a program as a tactic to avoid censorship limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Shutting down or eliminating a student newspaper/program can be used by administration as a way to avoid censorship rules, because 'you can't censor a student newspaper you no longer have.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPLC noted that schools increasingly shut down student newspapers as a form of censorship. Courts may scrutinize such tactics, but the tactic complicates constitutional remedies (and standing issues) if plaintiffs can no longer show ongoing injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate educational reason required to remove curricular publication opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing a class or program that publishes student work (e.g., a journalism class/newspaper) may violate free-speech rights unless the school can show a legitimate educational reason for the removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media-law attorneys argue that elimination of a student newspaper or curricular option that publishes award-winning material is problematic unless justified by legitimate pedagogical/educational reasons. This is an application of Hazelwood's pedagogical-justification principle to program elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common censorship triggers to watch for
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories critical of the school or perceived to make administrators look bad are common triggers for censorship or for more severe administrative responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPLC observed that the most common censorship trigger was a story that criticized the school or that the administration perceived as making them look bad, which often precipitates attempts to control content or eliminate programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadnaming and byline naming policies as discriminatory practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies requiring transgender students to use their birth names on bylines (deadnaming) can be coercive and discriminatory toward transgender student journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports the administration instructed staff to use birth names (a practice known as deadnaming) and students reported coercion, bullying, and threats to faculty advisors — facts that support claims of discriminatory motive and potential Title IX/constitutional concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Print media editorial autonomy (relevant precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Print media has constitutional protections to determine its editorial content (Miami Herald v. Tornillo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Miami Herald v. Tornillo addresses a different context (state regulation of newspapers), it is cited to note that print media historically have rights to determine editorial content; its principles are sometimes invoked in discussions of student press autonomy, though applicability may vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional and policy variance affects protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Local, state, and institutional laws and policies vary; some jurisdictions or school systems may lack laws or policies preventing incidents like the Viking Saga shutdown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYC Schools Chancellor's statement noted support for student expression but commentators observed that there may be no law or policy in many places preventing a similar shutdown; practitioners should check local statutes and board policies for protections or gaps.
